title: Design an Online Shopping Cart: User, Product, Cart, CartItem, Coupon/Discount, checkout flow, inventory check, payment integration.
topicTitle: LLD Problems: Parking Lot, Elevator, Chess, etc.
keyPoints: A Cart holds CartItems, each referencing a Product and a quantity; the subtotal is sum of price times quantity.
Discounts are pulled into a DiscountStrategy interface with implementations for flat, percentage, and buy-one-get-one promotions.
Checkout is the critical, must-be-atomic flow: validate inventory, apply discounts, charge payment, then decrement stock.
If payment fails, no stock is deducted; if stock is insufficient, no payment is taken.
The authoritative inventory check happens at checkout under a lock or atomic decrement, not when the item is first added to the cart.
All money is handled with BigDecimal to avoid floating-point rounding errors.
This is the same transactional discipline used at National Bank of India for purchasing limited assets like gold coins.

s1_definition.oneliner: A shopping cart totals items, applies discounts, validates inventory at checkout, and charges payment atomically.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **User** – the customer with an account and payment methods.
- **Product** – carries a name, price (`BigDecimal`), and available stock.
- **Cart** – holds a list of `CartItem` objects, each with a product and quantity.
- **CartItem** – references one Product and a quantity; contributes price times quantity to the subtotal.
- **DiscountStrategy** – a pluggable interface for flat, percentage, and buy-one-get-one promotions.
- **CheckoutService** – the atomic flow that validates inventory, applies discounts, charges payment, and decrements stock.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the shopping cart as a payment basket at National Bank of India's online store. Rajesh adds items to his basket, each with a quantity and price. When he checks out, the system totals the basket, applies any coupon he has, confirms the items are actually in stock, charges his account, and reduces inventory. The cart is just a running tally until checkout turns it into a real transaction.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Checkout Flow (must be atomic):
  ───────────────────────────────

  1. Validate inventory for every item
       │
       ▼ all in stock?
  2. Apply DiscountStrategy to subtotal
       │
       ▼
  3. PaymentStrategy.charge(userId, total)
       │
       ├── fails → abort (no stock deducted)
       │
       ▼ success
  4. Product.decrementStock(quantity)
       │
       ├── fails → PaymentStrategy.refund()
       │
       ▼ success
  5. Order created, cart cleared
```

```text
  Cart Structure:
  ───────────────

  Cart (RAJESH-001)
  ├── CartItem: Gold Coin  x 2  ₹1500 x 2 = ₹3000
  ├── CartItem: Silver Bar x 1  ₹500  x 1 = ₹500
  │                                    Subtotal: ₹3500
  │                              10% discount: -₹350
  └──────────────────────────────  Total: ₹3150
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
When you design an online shopping cart, model a User holding a Cart of cart items, where each item references a Product and a quantity, and the cart computes a running subtotal. The cart itself is just a tally; the real work and the real risk live in the checkout flow.

Discounts are the first place to apply good design. Pull coupon logic into a discount-strategy interface with implementations for flat, percentage, and buy-one-get-one promotions, so marketing can launch a new promotion as a new class rather than forcing a change to the checkout code. This is the Strategy pattern and the Open/Closed Principle together.

Checkout is the critical, must-be-atomic flow. It validates inventory for every item, applies discounts to compute the authoritative final total, charges payment, and only then decrements stock. The ordering matters: if payment fails, no stock is deducted, and if stock is insufficient, no payment is taken, so the system never ends up half-committed.

The subtle correctness concern is the race between adding to the cart and checking out, because an item can sell out in between. The authoritative inventory check and decrement happen at checkout under a lock or atomic operation, never when the item is first added. All money is `BigDecimal`. At National Bank of India, this is the same transactional discipline applied to any purchase of a limited asset like gold coins, where the inventory check, payment, and stock deduction must succeed or fail together as one unit.

Remember one sentence: a shopping cart totals items, applies discount strategies, and atomically validates inventory, charges payment, and decrements stock at checkout.
